content: Breastfeeding offers significant health benefits, and the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, continuing up to two years or beyond. However, lactational breast abscesses, which are localized collections of infected fluid within the breast tissue, often lead women to discontinue breastfeeding. These abscesses are typically managed using antibiotics, incision and drainage (I&D), or ultrasound-guided needle aspiration, but there is no established consensus on the most effective treatment approach. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various treatments for lactational breast abscesses in breastfeeding women. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared different interventions for treating lactational breast abscesses. Studies published only as abstracts, quasi-RCTs, and cluster-RCTs were excluded. Data were independently assessed by two reviewers, and the accuracy of the extracted data was verified. Six studies were included in the review, but only four studies involving 325 women provided data relevant to lactational breast abscesses. The overall quality of the included studies was limited, with an unclear risk of bias due to poor reporting. Two studies did not differentiate between lactational and non-lactational abscesses, and their data were excluded from the analysis. Needle Aspiration (with or without Ultrasound Guidance) vs. Incision and Drainage (I&D) Time to Complete Resolution: Three studies assessed the time required for complete resolution of the abscess. However, there was significant variability in the data (heterogeneity: Tau² = 47.63, I² = 97%), and subgroup differences (ultrasound-guided vs. non-ultrasound-guided) were evident (Chi² = 56.88, I² = 98.2%, p < 0.00001). Due to this heterogeneity, the data were not pooled for meta-analysis. One study reported that needle aspiration led to faster resolution compared to I&D (mean difference [MD] -6.07 days; 95% confidence interval [CI] -7.81 to -4.33; n = 36). However, 41% of women in the needle aspiration group were excluded due to treatment failure. Another study also favored needle aspiration, with a mean difference of -17.80 days (95% CI -21.27 to -14.33; n = 64), but 17% of women in the needle aspiration group were excluded due to treatment failure. A third study found a shorter resolution time with needle aspiration (MD -16.00 days; 95% CI -18.73 to -13.27; n = 60), but the number of women lost to follow-up was not reported, making the results unclear. Overall, the limitations in the data, including exclusions and unclear follow-up, make these findings inconclusive. Continuation of Breastfeeding: Two studies examined breastfeeding continuation after treatment. One study found that women treated with needle aspiration were more likely to continue breastfeeding (risk ratio [RR] 2.89; 95% CI 1.64 to 5.08; n = 60). The other study found no significant difference between the groups (RR 1.09; 95% CI 0.97 to 1.22; n = 70). Due to substantial heterogeneity (I² = 97%), the data were not pooled. Treatment Failure: Treatment failure was more common in the needle aspiration group compared to the I&D group (RR 16.12; 95% CI 2.21 to 117.73; two studies, n = 115). In one study, 9 out of 22 women in the needle aspiration group required subsequent I&D due to treatment failure. In another study, 6 out of 35 women in the needle aspiration group also required I&D. In contrast, all abscesses in the I&D group were successfully treated. Patient Satisfaction: One study (n = 60) reported that women in the needle aspiration group were more satisfied with their treatment compared to those who underwent I&D. Incision and Drainage (I&D) with or without Antibiotics Time to Resolution: One study (n = 150) compared the addition of a broad-spectrum cephalosporin (either a single dose or a course of treatment) to I&D. The mean time to resolution was similar across all groups: 7.3 days for women receiving a course of antibiotics, 6.9 days for women receiving a single dose of antibiotics, 7.4 days for women who did not receive antibiotics. Standard deviations, p-values, and confidence intervals were not reported, preventing further analysis. Treatment Failure: There was no significant difference in treatment failure rates between women who received antibiotics (single dose or course) and those who did not (RR 1.00; 95% CI 0.36 to 2.76). Post-Operative Complications: The risk of wound infections was similar between women who received antibiotics and those who did not (RR 0.58; 95% CI 0.29 to 1.17), regardless of whether they received a single dose or a course of antibiotics. Adverse Events and Secondary Outcomes The included studies provided limited data on secondary outcomes, including adverse events. No adverse events were reported in the studies. Additionally, data on breastfeeding continuation and other secondary outcomes were rarely reported. Authors' Conclusions The evidence is insufficient to determine whether needle aspiration is more effective than I&D for treating lactational breast abscesses. Similarly, there is no clear evidence to support the routine use of antibiotics in women undergoing I&D for lactational breast abscesses. The quality of evidence for the primary outcome of treatment failure was graded as low, primarily due to the inclusion of small studies with few events and an unclear risk of bias.
